es.text: más antiguas que se conocen. Lleva el nombre de Légal, un jugador francés del siglo XVIII. Su partida más citada la ganó en París a un rival llamado Saint Brie, y se suele fechar en 1750, aunque esa fecha es dudosa. La idea es atrevida: las blancas dejan su dama atacada y, a cambio, lanzan las piezas menores contra el rey negro, que sigue en el centro. Si las negras se llevan la dama sin mirar, pierden enseguida. Sale en aperturas abiertas, cuando el rey negro todavía no se ha enrocado y las piezas menores blancas ya están en juego. Lo que hay que recordar, sobre todo con negras: antes de capturar una pieza grande, pregúntate por qué el rival te la deja.

en.text: It is one of the oldest known

. It is named after Légal, a French player of the 18th century. His best-known game was a win in Paris against an opponent called Saint Brie, usually dated 1750, though that date is doubtful. The idea is bold: White lets the queen be taken and, in return, throws the minor pieces at the black king, which is still in the centre. If Black grabs the queen without looking, the game is over at once. It comes up in open games, while the black king has not castled yet and the white minor pieces are already out. What to remember, above all with Black: before you take a big piece, ask yourself why your opponent is letting you have it.

en.text: This position comes from a game between Richard Réti and Savielly Tartakower, played in Vienna in 1910. It lasted eleven moves and is still taught as an example of what it costs to leave the king in the centre. It began with a Caro-Kann Defence, where Black answers White’s king pawn advance by moving the queen’s bishop pawn one square. Black brought the queen out early and has just taken a knight, but the black king is still in the centre, without
. White, on the other hand, has already castled and has the pieces in play. The lesson: when the enemy king stays in the centre and your pieces are already out, look for
, even if they cost material. Counting pieces is of little use if the enemy king has nowhere to go.

en.text: Paul Morphy played this game in Paris in 1858, in a box at the opera while a performance was on stage. His opponents were two amateurs, Duke Karl II of Brunswick and Count Isouard, who chose Black’s moves together. It began with the Philidor Defence, named after the same Philidor as the rook ending. Today it is used to teach
: Morphy brings his pieces out fast and with threats, while Black trades off a bishop early, moves the queen twice and leaves the
rook at home. When the attack comes, White gives up first a knight and then a rook to open lines towards the black king, which still has not

Lleva el nombre de Georg Kieninger, que la jugó en una partida informal en Viena en 1925. Las blancas han ganado material y creen que lo peor ha pasado, pero su rey sigue en el centro, rodeado de sus propias piezas y sin casillas a las que huir. Es el terreno típico de las trampas de apertura: un rey sin enrocar y una pieza propia que parece defenderlo todo, pero que puede quedar

. Lo que hay que recordar es que una pieza clavada no puede capturar fuera de la línea de la clavada, así que las casillas que parecía defender quedan libres. Antes de capturar material en la apertura, mira qué piezas tuyas pueden quedar clavadas contra el rey y qué casillas le quedan libres a tu rey.

en.text: This trap comes from the Budapest

White has won material and thinks the worst is over, but the white king is still in the centre, surrounded by its own pieces and with no squares to run to. That is typical ground for opening traps: an uncastled king and one of its own pieces that seems to guard everything, but can end up

. What to remember is that a pinned piece cannot capture off the line of the pin, so the squares it seemed to guard are open. Before you grab material in the opening, check which of your pieces could end up pinned to the king and which squares your king has left.

es.text: En español se llama mate de la coz porque lo da el caballo, como una coz, contra un rey rodeado de sus propias piezas. Es un patrón muy antiguo: ya aparece en el libro de Luis Ramírez de Lucena de 1497. En inglés, una de sus versiones más conocidas se llama el legado de Philidor, aunque Lucena la recogió siglos antes. Suele darse contra un rey que se ha ido a la esquina después de

corto, con los peones de delante sin mover y sus propias piezas cerrándole las salidas. Las señales que hay que buscar son un rey sin casillas libres y un caballo rival que puede llegar a darle jaque. Para defenderte, dale a tiempo una salida a tu rey: un peón movido delante del enroque basta muchas veces para que el caballo no pueda rematar.

en.text: In Spanish it is called the kick mate, because the knight delivers it like a horse’s kick against a king hemmed in by its own pieces. It is a very old pattern: it already appears in Luis Ramírez de Lucena’s book of 1497. In English, one of its best-known versions is called Philidor’s Legacy, although Lucena recorded it centuries earlier. It usually happens to a king that has gone to the corner after

short, with the pawns in front unmoved and its own pieces blocking the exits. The signs to look for are a king with no free squares and an enemy knight that can reach a checking square. To defend, give your king a way out in time: one pawn moved in front of the castled king is often enough to stop the knight from finishing.

No fue el primero en darlo: se conoce una partida anterior, Horwitz contra Popert, jugada en Hamburgo en 1844. en.text: This mate is named after Samuel Boden, an English player, who delivered it in this game against Schulder in London in 1853. He was not the first: an earlier game is known, Horwitz against Popert, played in Hamburg in 1844. The pattern is easy to spot: two bishops crossing on different diagonals, like a pair of scissors, in front of a king that has

long. For it to work, the squares around the king must be taken by its own pieces, which take away its exits instead of protecting it. What to remember: if you castle long, watch the diagonals that reach your king, and do not surround it with pieces that block its way. A king with free squares is much harder to mate.

es.text: El mate del pasillo es de los primeros que hay que conocer, porque se cuela en partidas de todos los niveles. El nombre describe bien la situación: el rey está encerrado en su
por sus propios peones, como al fondo de un pasillo, y una torre o la dama rival entra por esa fila y da
. Suele aparecer en el medio juego y en los finales con torres, cuando ya se han cambiado piezas y queda poca gente vigilando esa fila. La lucha suele estar en una

: gana quien tenga más piezas apuntando a la casilla por la que se entra en la última fila. Para prevenirlo, basta con mover a tiempo uno de los peones de delante del rey y abrirle una casilla de escape. Parece una jugada perdida, pero salva muchas partidas.

en.text: The back-rank mate is one of the first mates to learn, because it sneaks into games at every level. The rook or queen comes in along the
, where the king is shut in by its own pawns, and delivers
. It usually turns up in the middlegame and in rook endings, once pieces have been traded and few of them are left watching that rank. The fight is usually over an

: whoever has more pieces aimed at the square where the file meets the back rank wins it. To prevent it, all it takes is moving one of the pawns in front of the king in time, to give it an escape square. It looks like a wasted move, but it saves a lot of games.

Heinse la tomó, al parecer, de un texto del italiano Giambattista Lolli. El patrón necesita tres piezas: un caballo que vigila dos casillas de huida del rey, un peón del propio rey que le tapa otra, y una torre que llega por la columna del borde para dar

. Aparece cuando el rey se ha refugiado en la esquina y esa columna se puede abrir, a veces a cambio de mucho material. Lo que hay que recordar: un caballo cerca de un rey arrinconado es una pieza muy peligrosa, aunque no parezca atacar nada. Si tienes uno ahí, mira si puedes llevar una torre a la columna del borde. Y si el rey arrinconado es el tuyo, no dejes que esa columna se abra.

en.text: The name comes from a German novel, Anastasia und das Schachspiel, by Wilhelm Heinse, in which this position appears. Heinse apparently took it from a text by the Italian Giambattista Lolli. The pattern needs three pieces: a knight covering two of the king’s escape squares, one of the king’s own pawns blocking another, and a rook coming down the edge file to deliver

. It turns up when the king has taken shelter in the corner and that file can be opened, sometimes at the cost of a lot of material. What to remember: a knight near a cornered king is a very dangerous piece even if it seems to attack nothing. If you have one there, see whether you can bring a rook to the edge file. And if the cornered king is yours, do not let that file open.

es.text: Es uno de los mates más antiguos que se conocen: ya aparece en manuscritos árabes de la Edad Media, cuando se jugaba al shatranj, el antepasado directo del ajedrez moderno. En aquel juego la torre y el caballo se movían igual que hoy, así que este mate, que solo usa esas dos piezas, ha llegado sin cambios hasta nosotros. El patrón es sencillo. La torre da

pegada al rey, en el borde del tablero, y el caballo la protege y además vigila la casilla por la que el rey podría escapar. El rey tiene que estar en una esquina o muy cerca, sin salidas. Tener más material no sirve de nada si la próxima jugada del rival es
. Lo que hay que recordar: antes de contar piezas, comprueba si tu rey está a salvo, y un caballo rival cerca de tu esquina siempre merece una mirada.

en.text: It is one of the oldest known mates: it already appears in medieval Arabic manuscripts, from the days of shatranj, the direct ancestor of modern chess. In that game the rook and the knight moved just as they do today, so this mate, which uses only those two pieces, has come down to us unchanged. The pattern is simple. The rook gives

right next to the king, on the edge of the board, and the knight protects it and also covers the square the king could flee to. The king has to be in a corner or very close to one, with no way out. Being ahead in material is worthless if the opponent’s next move is
. What to remember: before you count pieces, check that your king is safe, and an enemy knight near your corner always deserves a look.

es.text: Hay clavada cuando una pieza no puede moverse sin dejar al descubierto otra más valiosa que está detrás. La
contra el rey es la más fuerte: la pieza clavada no puede salirse de la línea, porque las reglas no permiten dejar al propio rey en

Solo clavan las piezas que se mueven en línea recta: el alfil por las diagonales, la torre por filas y columnas, y la dama por todas. Las columnas abiertas y las diagonales que llevan al rey son los lugares típicos. Lo que hay que recordar: si tu dama y tu rey están en la misma línea, aunque haya piezas en medio, revisa si una torre o un alfil rival puede plantarse en ella. Y si vas a clavar algo valioso, comprueba antes que la casilla desde la que clavas está protegida.

en.text: A pin happens when a piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable one behind it. A
against the king is the strongest kind: the pinned piece cannot leave the line, because the rules do not allow you to leave your own king in

. It can only move along it, which includes taking the pinning piece if it can reach it. Only pieces that move in straight lines can pin: the bishop along diagonals, the rook along ranks and files, and the queen along all of them. Open files and diagonals leading to the king are the typical places. What to remember: if your queen and your king are on the same line, even with pieces in between, check whether an enemy rook or bishop can settle on it. And when you pin something valuable, first make sure the square you pin from is protected.

en.text: is a pin the other way round. The piece under attack is the more valuable one, usually the king, and when it steps aside it exposes another piece standing behind it on the same line. If the attack is a

It is common in endings, when few pieces are left and the king comes out of its shelter to play on open ranks and files. What to remember: if the enemy king and queen are on the same rank, file or diagonal, look for a check along that line. And when you defend, avoid lining up your king with your queen or another valuable piece.
